item.title: When Imposter Syndrome Is Actually Misalignment
item.description:
Imposter Syndrome

When Imposter Syndrome Is Actually Misalignment

The hidden psychology behind feeling like a fraud when success loses its soul.

Posted July 5, 2026

Key points
  • Imposter syndrome may be misalignment, not low confidence.
  • Cognitive dissonance rises when values and behaviors don't match.
  • Selling loses integrity when service becomes pressure or manipulation.
  • Congruence creates deeper confidence than performance ever can.

I was recently in a room filled with successful entrepreneurs, leaders, and creators. Many had built companies, generated serious revenue, led teams, created influence, and achieved what most people would clearly define as success.

At one point, the facilitator asked, “Raise your hand if you’ve ever felt imposter syndrome.” Every hand in the room went up. Everyone laughed, because it was both ridiculous and painfully honest. How could so many capable, accomplished, heart-centered leaders still feel like imposters?

The common explanation is that imposter syndrome means you are failing to internalize your success. You have the results, but you still secretly fear that someone is going to find out you're not as competent, talented, or qualified as they think you are.

There is truth in that explanation. The original research on the impostor phenomenon described high-achieving people who struggled with an internal sense of intellectual phoniness despite objective evidence of accomplishment (Clance & Imes, 1978). A systematic review published in the Journal of General Internal Medicine found that prevalence estimates ranged greatly from 9% to 82%, depending on the population studied and the assessment tool used (Bravata et al., 2020).

So yes, imposter syndrome is common. And there’s another layer we do not talk about enough. Often, what we call imposter syndrome is an alignment problem, not a confidence problem.

Source: pexels/andreapiacquadio

The Dissonance Beneath the Doubt

Cognitive dissonance is the psychological discomfort that arises when our beliefs, values, and behaviors do not match (Festinger, 1957). It’s what happens when the life you’re performing starts contradicting the truth you actually believe.

This shows up everywhere in modern leadership. A leader says they want to serve, but they’re secretly trying to manipulate people into buying. A coach says they want to help people transform, yet most of their energy is going into the 4 Ps: persuasion, pressure, positioning, and proving. A leader says they care about impact, but they’re more obsessed with optics and sales numbers than with whether their work is actually helping people.

This slippery slope is easy to get pulled down in a world that constantly rewards performance over presence. Yet the body keeps the score. Your nervous system feels the split before your mind tries to rationalize it. The feeling may be a signal that the means of success are no longer aligned with the person pursuing it.

When Selling Loses Its Servant Heart

Being ambitious and desiring a successful business aren’t spiritual crimes. And there’s nothing inherently wrong with selling, marketing, or making money. Thank goodness, because most of us still enjoy quality food, shelter, and the occasional overpriced smoothie.

The problem is when selling loses its servant heart. There’s a difference between inviting someone into transformation and manipulating them into a decision. Between clearly communicating value and performing certainty you don’t actually feel. And between creating honest urgency and using fear to push someone across the finish line.

article continues after advertisement

When people build success through pressure, performance, exaggeration, or emotional manipulation, the nervous system often registers that conflict. The outer world may be applauding, but the inner world starts whispering, “This doesn’t feel clean.” Sometimes that’s integrity trying to get your attention rather than imposter syndrome. Read that again…

I learned this lesson the hard way the summer before my junior year of college. I made a last-minute decision to study abroad in London through Boston University’s Internship Programme, and I needed money fast. So I took a job in a smoke-filled, windowless call center selling magazine subscriptions through an automated, manipulative script. The offer was three monthly magazines “free,” followed by a $757, five-year commitment to a weekly magazine like U.S. News & World Report.

I got very good at it. Too good, probably. I broke national records by selling 52 packages in one week and made over $8,000 in personal profit in six weeks. That job funded my London dream, yet it also gave me an early education in the difference between desire and integrity. I was committed, hungry, and willing to work. And I started having nightmares about it because deep down I also knew there is a difference between helping someone and getting someone.

The deeper lesson stayed with me: chasing a dream is powerful, yet if the path to the dream requires you to leave your servant heart behind, the success may cost more than the price tag suggests.

The Moving Target of Success

Many high achievers feel like imposters because they are chasing a target that constantly moves. More money, clients, visibility, or followers. More proof that they have finally made it. Yet there’s no arrival when the scoreboard keeps changing.

Social comparison theory suggests that humans naturally evaluate themselves in relation to others (Festinger, 1954). Every scroll gives your mind another person to measure against: their launch, their body, their relationship, their revenue, their audience, their retreat, their podcast, or their perfectly lit “candid” kitchen photo. This is the illness of comparative-itis.

article continues after advertisement

It turns progress into inadequacy and makes enough feel like almost. And when success is measured only by money, followers, sales, and status, something inside eventually starts to revolt because everything feels incomplete. External success is only one dimension of real wealth. Real wealth also includes health, relationships, integrity, peace, purpose, contribution, freedom, and the ability to look in the mirror without abandoning yourself.

When people only chase external metrics, they may start making choices that move them farther from who they actually want to be. Over time, that gap creates dissonance. The mind may interpret that dissonance as, “I’m an imposter,” when the deeper message is, “I’ve outgrown this version of success.”

Master the Inner Split

In my E.M.P.O.W.E.R. Process, this connects deeply to Master. Mastery is about developing the self-awareness to recognize where your inner world and outer behavior are no longer aligned. It's easy to blame imposter syndrome on low confidence. It's harder and more powerful to ask, “Where am I participating in the very thing that makes me feel false?”

Mastery requires emotional honesty. Take three minutes to journal on these three questions:

Am I serving or performing?

Am I marketing from truth or manipulating from fear?

Am I measuring my life by what actually matters, or by what gets the most applause?

These questions are uncomfortable because they cut through the performance and bring the conversation back to responsibility.

The Return to Congruence

Congruence means your actions, values, message, and methods start telling the same story. You can sell with integrity, market with honesty, and lead with ambition without making money your god. When leaders return to service, the inner split begins to heal.

The next time imposter syndrome shows up, do not immediately try to silence it with affirmations or achievement receipts. Instead, pause and ask yourself:

article continues after advertisement

“Is this self-doubt, or is this misalignment?”

Then ask:

“What part of my life, business, leadership, or success strategy no longer feels true?”

That question can change everything.

Sometimes, you need to more fully own your competence, stop discounting your gifts, and finally accept that you belong in the room. And other times, you need to stop betraying your values in order to stay in the room.

The Bottom Line

Sometimes, imposter syndrome is a signal that your definition of success has become too narrow, external, or disconnected from service. The goal is to create success you can actually feel proud to claim. Because real confidence comes from becoming congruent enough that you no longer have to wonder which version of you is going to show up.

item.title: The Illusion of Expertise
item.description:
Confidence

The Illusion of Expertise

How the appearance of mastery disarms natural skepticism.

Posted July 5, 2026

Key points
  • Humans are uniquely wired to learn from each other, but we also have robust defenses against deception.
  • The real magician’s trick is to turn a room full of skeptics into a fully immersed audience.
  • We often need to tell whether someone is an expert in a field in which we ourselves are not experts.

Like many other startups during the deepest stretch of COVID lockdowns, we decided on a remote team-building experience to keep our spirits up. Soon, 10 of us appeared on a Zoom call, staring at our webcams, waiting for a virtual magician to arrive.

Magician is a tough career choice. It takes way too much practice just to get started, and there's very little margin for error. People in the audience are watching closely for mistakes, hoping to find out how a trick works.

To do all of this online puts the bar impossibly high. My generation grew up watching movies with awe-inspiring computer graphics, and played video games that look realer than real. So if we encounter something on-screen with no obvious explanation, we will safely write off the absolute best illusion and impeccable sleight of hand as some kind of internet trickery.

Needless to say, our virtual magician had his job cut out for him. We were a highly skeptical audience on high alert, arriving with the shared assumption that we could deconstruct whatever was about to happen on screen.

The instructions told us to bring our own pack of cards to the show. When it came to the main act, we picked a random card, looked at it, and were in for a big surprise: The illusionist accurately guessed the cards exactly as only we could see them. He certainly couldn’t have seen the deck I’d bought at the corner store just that morning. There were no mirrors, no shiny surfaces, no reflections in our glasses. It was, for all intents and purposes, magic.

It was great fun, even though we were left hanging as far as finding out how the trick went. We may never learn that thanks to the magician’s code, but there’s at least one type of magic we can discuss here: the one to do with social dynamics.

A group of skeptical individuals all let our guards down, as the illusionist, in turn, got each of us on his side. We didn’t forget that we were being tricked; we became a giddy, fully immersed group, willingly surrendering to the performance. Quite the skill in any social situation!

Bypassing our firewalls

Evolutionary psychologists point out that while humans are uniquely wired to learn from each other, we also have robust defense mechanisms against deception. According to cognitive scientist Dan Sperber and his colleagues, we possess a filter called “epistemic vigilance.” This suite of cognitive mechanisms is designed to evaluate whether a source of information is trustworthy, and whether their claim makes sense.

When we observe someone at work, we process information on multiple tracks. Watching the magician on our Zoom call, our explicit, focal attention was busy trying to catch the smallest sign of cheating. At the same time, our implicit processing was absorbing the magician’s tone of voice, his pacing, his perfectly smooth transitions, and his total absence of hesitation.

A great illusion relies on exploiting cognitive blind spots, but that’s just half the job. How we actually experience the illusion relies heavily on our skepticism or feelings.

The magician didn’t need to break our vigilance; his job was to bypass it by providing the kind of proxy signals that we intuitively associate with high competence—things like smoothness, confidence, or rhythm. Breaking down these walls is what makes the show great. If an audience stays in a state of high alert, the performance devolves into an interrogation, which is way less fun than a willing, collaborative audience, ready to experience wonder.

Masters at work

To understand just how heavily our brains weigh the appearance of mastery, we can read a study published by researcher and professor Chia-Jung Tsay. Her team wanted to know exactly how people evaluate expertise, so she asked both novice and professional musicians to identify competition winners of high-level classical music performances. The participants were divided into three groups. One group only listened to the audio. Another group watched the video with the sound on. The third group watched a completely silent video.

article continues after advertisement

You might think that the expert musicians who listened to the pristine audio of a piano concerto would be the most accurate at identifying a superior performance. You'd be wrong: Both the novices and the professionals were most accurate at identifying the winners after watching the silent video.

Unable to hear a single note, the participants could only read the meta-signals of physical confidence, passion, and fluid movement. In evaluating the performance, these visual cues of mastery turned out to be more important than the actual technical output of the music.

This is what was at play on our Zoom call with the magician. We thought we were “listening to the notes” by trying to dissect each trick, but on a subconscious level, a part of our brain may as well have been “watching the silent video.” The magician's pacing and the absolute smoothness of his delivery signaled a level of fluency that served as a proxy for competence. These factors didn’t contribute to the trick mechanically, but they helped disarm our inner skeptics.

To be recognized as masters in our own fields, we have to learn this exact type of signaling. The problem is, we tend to spend the vast majority of our time perfecting the explicit mechanics of the job, assuming that if the substance is sound, our competence will be obvious to our peers. But as the silent-video study suggests, audiences lean heavily on fluency as a shortcut. Taking the time to practice a smooth delivery isn’t just superficial polish. Hesitation or backtracking inadvertently signals a lack of competence, forcing an audience’s epistemic filters to work overtime. A seamless delivery, on the other hand, allows their inner skeptics to relax and focus on the actual experience.

item.title: The Ethical Conditions of Dialogue-Play and Understanding
item.description:
Philosophy

The Ethical Conditions of Dialogue-Play and Understanding

What commitments are needed for the process of understanding to take place?

Posted July 5, 2026

Key points
  • Genuine dialogue and understanding require that certain ethical conditions be met.
  • The interlocutor must take seriously what the other person says as a claim to truth worth learning.
  • The interlocutor must approach the other with respect and a good will to understand.

This post is Part 3 of a series.

In my first post of this series, I introduced Hans-Georg Gadamer’s way of seeing human understanding as a process of play—a back-and-forth communicative movement in which human beings reach a shared grasp of some subject matter of their world together. In my second post, I outlined eight key characteristics of this movement of play, highlighting how it is a collaborative, free, unpredictable, and open-ended movement in which participants are transformed and enriched.

What has always caught my interest in Gadamer’s description of the dialogical play-process is that it requires (what I call) certain “ethical conditions” to be met. There are particular ways we must approach and treat another person, and the “game” itself, for a genuine dialogue to take place and for a shared understanding to emerge. There are commitments, responsibilities, and a self-disciplined conduct necessary for genuine dialogue and understanding to occur.

In this post, I want to show how those ethical conditions emerge from Gadamer’s description of play. I also want to begin to consider if illuminating these ethical conditions gives us a clue as to why dialogue and understanding so often fail in our culture today.

Taking the Game of Understanding Seriously

First of all, Gadamer observes that a player in any game has to take the game seriously for the game to function. They have to engage fully, rather than stand back at a distance or view the activity as “just a game.” If the player does not take the game seriously, Gadamer observes, we call them a “spoilsport,” and the collaborative, back-and-forth activity cannot get underway.

The interlocutor in dialogue-play must, accordingly, take the game of understanding seriously. In particular, they must take seriously what the other has to say as a “claim to truth” about our world—a claim to truth that’s worthy of a hearing and worthy of grasping.

That means, as interlocutors, we must respect the other who speaks with us as someone who has something meaningful to say, and who has some insight to share from their own experience, which might be quite different from what we already think but can contribute to our knowledge.

We must approach the other with a “good will to understand,” rather than a will to simply refute the other or convince them of our own beliefs. We must be open to what the other has to say for genuine dialogue and understanding to function.

Risking Our Prejudgments

Second, just as a player in any game must take risks, the interlocutor in dialogue-play must be ready and willing to risk their own prejudgments (their preconceptions or preconceived notions) about the subject matter under discussion and find out that their old judgments might have been wrong, incomplete, or in need of revision.

article continues after advertisement

Gadamer says: “Our own prejudice is properly brought into play by being put at risk. Only by being given full play is it able to experience the other’s claim to truth and make possible for him to have full play himself” (Truth and Method, 299).

That means the interlocutor must be willing to “try out” their beliefs in the conversation and in the process “be tried,” tested, and challenged. The interlocutor must, in other words, be open to learning from the other and transforming their own understanding based on what the other says.

Gadamer explains: “To reach an understanding in a dialogue is not merely a matter of putting oneself forward and successfully asserting one’s own point of view, but [it’s a matter of] being transformed into a communion in which we do not remain what we were" (TM, 379).

Losing Oneself in the Game of Understanding

Finally, the interlocutors must be willing to lose themselves in the conversation. This means that the interlocutors must be willing to give up control in the conversation and let the subject matter and its truth be their guide.

They must not try to control the other in the conversation by aiming to silence them, “make” them believe their own view, or “beat them” in a debate. These are game-stopping moves that shut down the play of dialogue and understanding.

Gadamer says: “To conduct a conversation means to allow oneself to be conducted by the subject matter to which the partners in the dialogue are oriented. It requires that one does not try to argue the other person down but that one really considers the weight [of what they have said]” (TM, 367).

For Gadamer, those who are truly skilled dialogue partners know how to give up control. They know how to open themselves not only to the other, but to the subject matter and its truth—whether that truth confirms and enriches what they previously believed, or corrects and significantly alters it.

article continues after advertisement

Openness to the Other

You may have noticed that the idea of being “open” came up a lot in this discussion of how interlocutors need to comport themselves toward each other and toward the game of dialogue-play for it to function.

This phrase “openness to the other” captures in a general sense the ethical conditions of dialogue-play and understanding.

Speaking of this openness, Gadamer says: “In human relations the important thing is, as we have seen, to experience the Thou truly as a Thou—i.e., not to overlook his claim but to let him really say something to us. Here is where openness belongs ... Without such openness to one another there is no genuine human bond” (TM, 361).

Using Martin Buber’s language of “I and Thou,” Gadamer begins to show here how the approach of openness to the other forms the moral connection (the genuine human bond), that makes dialogue and a shared understanding possible.

Gadamer distinguishes the “open” approach to the other from three other approaches, which he thinks have become quite popular in the modern age but are problematic. I have labeled them the scientific, psychological, and sophistic approaches to the other. All three of these problematic approaches are characterized not by openness, but by postures of closedness, distance, and dominance, which destroy the moral bond, sabotage the movement of play, degrade dialogue, and keep genuine understanding from taking place. In the next post, we’ll look at these three problematic approaches to the other, which (I sense) have become our cultural norms.
